profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal troubleshooting meeting at a software company piloting an LLM-driven automated debugging service inspired by scientific debugging. Overnight, the AutoSD-based service began producing patch explanations that look coherent but are inconsistent across reruns, and several explanations reference observations that do not match what engineers see when replaying the bug locally. The meeting is between the engineer responsible for the AutoSD reasoning pipeline and the engineer responsible for the CI execution/debugging infrastructure. Their agenda is to diagnose why explanations and confidence labels drift between runs on the same reported bug, identify the most plausible root cause, and agree on an immediate containment step before a demo to the developer-tools group later that day. The expected outcome is a short-term mitigation plan and a shared diagnosis of where the inconsistency is entering the pipeline.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: LLM prompting pipelines, automated program repair, explanation generation, evaluation on repair benchmarks
members.background: Priya built most of the AutoSD orchestration layer that generates hypotheses, drives debugger interactions, and produces natural-language rationales for candidate patches; she mostly works with benchmark-style bug datasets and local replay tooling.
members.private_state: Priya wants to show that the explanation layer is not the source of the incident because the pilot depends on trust in intelligible rationales; she is worried that people will blame the LLM reasoning loop when the real issue may be execution drift, but she also wants a quick mitigation that does not require changing the prompting pipeline right before the demo.
hidden_assumptions: If a bug is 'reproduced,' it is sufficient that the same bug-revealing test ends in the same assertion failure, even if intermediate traces differ somewhat.
When people mention 'yesterday's benchmark run,' they mean the curated Python subset run from the autosd-explainer branch that she reviewed for explanation quality.
Freezing the environment mainly means pinning the prompt template, tool-call order, and model version so the reasoning process is stable.
A 'same test' replay refers to the isolated bug-revealing test function used by AutoSD during hypothesis checking, not necessarily the entire CI test file with all fixtures and ordering effects.

members.name: Ethan Cole
members.role: Senior Backend Platform Engineer, CI and Runtime Tooling
members.expertise: Build and test infrastructure, containers, debugger instrumentation, flaky test diagnosis, runtime observability
members.background: Ethan owns the CI shards, sandbox images, and the headless debugger/trace collector that AutoSD invokes during repair attempts; he thinks in terms of deterministic execution environments and production-style reproducibility.
members.private_state: Ethan wants to prevent an unreliable system from being shown to the developer-tools group, and he is looking for the smallest operational change that restores determinism; he suspects that the pipeline is reading traces under conditions different from the original failing CI run, but he does not want to derail the meeting into a broader discussion about model behavior.
hidden_assumptions: If a bug is 'reproduced,' it means the replay matches the original CI shard behavior closely enough that the same execution path and debugger observations should appear.
When someone says 'yesterday's benchmark run,' they mean the nightly main-branch repair sweep that runs through the standard CI harness and feeds the dashboard.
Freezing the environment includes pinning the full container image, Python minor version, debugger build, environment variables, and test-order seed.
A 'same test' replay means rerunning the same failing test file under the CI harness so fixtures, module import state, and ordering remain comparable to the original failure.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as reproducing the bug
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they need to 'reproduce the failure' before trusting the explanation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means rerunning the bug-revealing test until it ends in the same failing assertion, which is enough to validate the hypothesis/explanation loop.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means recreating the original CI execution closely enough that the same execution path and debugger evidence appear, not just the same final assertion.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting conversations, 'reproduce the failure' sounds standard and uncontroversial; both assume the other shares the customary meaning from their own workflow, and neither hears anything obviously inconsistent on the surface.

misalignment_points.topic: Which run from yesterday they are talking about
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the run from yesterday' or 'yesterday's benchmark run' as evidence about when the issue started.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of a manually launched Python benchmark subset on the autosd-explainer branch used to inspect rationale quality.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the nightly main-branch CI repair sweep across the standard harness that populates the internal dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both runs happened yesterday, both involved AutoSD, and each engineer only regularly monitors one of them, so the shorthand sounds precise enough to each speaker without triggering a clarification request.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to freeze the environment
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that they should 'freeze the environment' to stop explanation drift.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes only the reasoning-layer ingredients: model version, prompt template, tool-call sequence, and hypothesis loop parameters.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the entire runtime envelope: container image, debugger binary, Python version, environment variables, and test-order seed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Freezing an environment is a familiar mitigation phrase, and each person's scope feels like the obvious default in their area; the phrase creates false consensus because both scopes are plausible and partially overlapping.

misalignment_points.topic: What they mean by rerunning the same test
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both suggest rerunning 'the same test under the debugger' to verify the root cause.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means the isolated bug-revealing test function that AutoSD extracted and replays during hypothesis checks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means the original failing test file as executed by the CI harness, including fixtures and surrounding test setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same shorthand because each believes the relevant test identity is already established by the incident ticket; the distinction between isolated test function and CI-harness replay remains implicit unless someone explicitly discusses fixture behavior.

turns.inner_thought: The explanations are the visible symptom, so I need to frame this carefully. On my side, when I say reproduce the failure, I mean getting the bug-revealing test to hit the same assertion again; that tells me the explanation loop is grounded enough to inspect. I really do not want this meeting to drift into 'the LLM made things up' when the more likely issue is that the runtime observations feeding it changed underneath us. And with the demo later, I need a mitigation that does not involve rewriting prompts or touching the orchestration path.

Overnight we had a few AutoSD cases where the explanations were internally coherent, but if you reran them, the rationale and confidence shifted around in ways that shouldn't happen. Before we decide anything about the demo, I think we need to reproduce the failure and see where the inconsistency is actually entering.

turns.inner_thought: The dashboard made this obvious in the nightly main-branch sweep, and what worries me is that the trace collector output no longer matches what the explanation cites. When I say yesterday's benchmark run, I mean that standard CI-harness repair sweep, not some ad hoc branch run. I want to keep this operational: if the execution context drifted, we can contain it without arguing about model cognition.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I first noticed it in yesterday's benchmark run on the dashboard. The explanation is pointing at observations that don't line up with what the trace collector stored, so from my side the mismatch shows up before anyone reads the natural-language summary.

turns.inner_thought: In yesterday's run, the one I reviewed was the Python subset on the autosd-explainer branch, and I saw the same failing assertion twice there. So to me this doesn't look like the explanation layer inventing facts from nothing; it looks like it is being fed slightly different observations across reruns. I should emphasize that distinction without making it sound like I'm defending my code at all costs.
turns.utterance: That's consistent with what I saw in yesterday's run too. I saw the same failing assertion twice, which is why I'm leaning toward the explanation pipeline consuming slightly different observations rather than just inventing them.

turns.inner_thought: If we're going to trust any explanation, we need to rerun the same test under the debugger the way CI actually executed it, with fixtures and ordering intact, and compare that trace to the stored artifact. Reproducing the failure means matching the original execution path closely enough that the debugger observations line up, not merely ending in the same assertion. I need to steer us to that without making this sound bigger than today's containment.
turns.utterance: Right. If we want to trust the explanation at all, I'd start by rerunning the same test under the debugger exactly as CI saw it, then compare that trace against the stored artifact. For me that's the fastest way to reproduce the failure in a way we can rely on.

turns.inner_thought: Freezing the environment is a good frame because I can keep the mitigation centered on the reasoning layer: pin the model version, prompt template, tool-call order, and hypothesis loop parameters so explanation behavior stops drifting while we inspect one bug. That avoids a risky pipeline change right before the demo and protects the explanation layer from being blamed prematurely.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For today's mitigation, I think we should freeze the environment so the hypothesis generation path and tool-call sequence stay stable while we inspect one representative bug end to end.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on freezing the environment. From my side that means pinning the full sandbox image, debugger build, Python minor version, environment variables, and test-order seed before I rerun the same test from the incident. That's the smallest operational change likely to restore determinism. If that settles the traces, we may not need to touch the model path at all.
turns.utterance: Agreed, freezing the environment is the right move. I can pin the sandbox image and the replay seed first, then rerun the same test and see whether the trace settles down.

turns.inner_thought: What I'm seeing locally is that the isolated bug-revealing test still fails in the same place, which to me strongly suggests AutoSD is reaching the same bug conclusion but with small observation differences across runs. That's exactly the kind of thing that can perturb rationales and confidence labels without meaning the explanation loop is hallucinating. I should say that plainly but still in shared language.

So the top-line behavior looks stable even if the supporting evidence isn't.

turns.inner_thought: On the dashboard, the nightly run only went unstable after the CI base image rotation. That's a huge clue. To me that points to execution drift caused by environment changes, which is exactly why freezing the environment needs to include the whole runtime envelope, not just reasoning settings. I don't want to turn this into a broad debate about model behavior when the timeline already implicates infrastructure.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with an execution-drift diagnosis as long as we don't knee-jerk disable explanations before checking one clean case. For the demo, I'd rather keep explanations enabled and gate on whether we can reproduce the failure consistently after freezing the environment for a representative bug. If that works, I can defend the explanation layer without touching prompts today.
turns.utterance: I think that's a reasonable working theory. For the demo, I'd prefer to keep explanations enabled but gate on whether we can reproduce the failure consistently after freezing the environment for one bug case.
